newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court sides with Florida in tobacco case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court sides with Florida in tobacco case.

text.p: The Supreme Court dealt a setback to the tobacco industry Monday by rejecting a challenge to a Florida law that allows the state to sue cigarette makers for the cost of smoking-related illnesses.

The high court rejected an appeal by Philip Morris Cos. Inc., the world's largest cigarette maker, and by Associated Industries of Florida Inc., one of the state's biggest business groups, urging that the 1994 law be declared unconstitutional.
Their lawyers had argued in the appeal that the law violates the constitutional protections of due process by stripping from businesses their traditional defences against product liability.

But the justices, turning down the appeal without comment or dissent, let stand a Florida Supreme Court ruling that the state has the legal right to sue cigarette makers for Medicaid costs incurred by Florida from tobacco-related illnesses.
The Supreme Court action did not create a nationwide precedent, but cleared the way for Florida's case to proceed. A trial has been set for August.

The high court's action also may provide a boost to 21 similar state lawsuits brought against the tobacco industry. Suits also have been filed by several local governments such as New York City and the counties of Los Angeles and San Francisco.
In New York, Philip Morris said it still believed the law was unconstitutional and left open the possibility of bringing another challenge later.

"This decision not to review the Florida law is not a ruling on the merits of our constitutional challenge and does not in any way affect our ability to seek a review in the future if that becomes necessary," Gregory Little, the company's senior assistant general counsel, said.
Philip Morris said it believed that Florida's lawsuit "is without legal merit," and said the state still faces "several significant legal obstacles" before the case can go to trial.
"Even with the state's blatant attempt to stack the deck against anyone it sues under the statute, we do not believe the state can carry its burden of proof," Little said.
Shares of tobacco companies tumbled on the news.
Philip Morris fell $3.50 to $125.625, RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. lost $1.375 to $32.50 and Loews Corp. dropped $2.125 to $101.50.

Sanford Bernstein analyst Gary Black said the Supreme Court rarely accepts a case prior to trial. "I don't know why the market cares about it because I don't think anyone expected the U.S. Supreme Court to take it on," he said.

But the ruling came on the heels of a ruling on Thursday by Mississippi's Supreme Court throwing out challenges by the state's governor and the tobacco industry that would have kept a $940 million case from proceeding to trial in June. That ruling also sent cigarette makers' stocks reeling.

Florida's civil lawsuit, filed in February 1995, seeks damages totalling nearly $1 billion. State officials estimated the Medicaid costs incurred by Florida to treat tobacco-related illnesses at more than $400 million a year.
The Florida Supreme Court in a 4-3 decision in June said the state could sue under the law.
The law stripped away the tobacco industry's traditional defence that smokers share the blame for their health problems because they made a personal choice to accept the risks.
It allowed the state to use statistical evidence to try to prove that tobacco was responsible for some of the illnesses.
In their challenge, Philip Morris and the state business group claimed the law was intended to "stack the deck" against tobacco firms and make sure the state won its lawsuit for monetary damages.

"It is as though the state has declared that in football league games, when the state university team's offence is on the field, the opponent's defence must withdraw to the sidelines," Philip Morris and the business group said.

They acknowledged the tobacco industry had become "unpopular" with certain segments of public opinion and certain government officials, but said the high court "is particularly vigilant" to protect the rights of unpopular groups.
Florida urged the justices to deny the appeal, saying the law represented a sound attempt for force tobacco companies to pay some of the social costs stemming from their actions.
"Whether an individual smoker has assumed the risk of smoking is simply immaterial to the tobacco company's liability to the state," Attorney General Robert Butterworth said.
